human.reader_value.reason: The chronic-gap finding becomes useful through a revealing comparison: French revenue is high relative to peers, while cash benefits and public-sector pay account for most of the spending difference. This improves understanding of high debt, but the commissioned crisis question is only partly answered because urgency, market pressure and political blockage remain outside the evidence.

human.explanation_argument.reason: The sequence from persistent deficits to accumulated debt, peer comparison and spending composition is understandable. Important limits are stated, including the benefits-category boundary and the debt/GDP denominator. However, “Between shocks it did not fall back” conflicts with the later explanation and chart of a falling debt ratio; “Low revenue is not the explanation” also treats a relative revenue level as a stronger exclusion of policy alternatives than the comparison establishes.

It leaves the central crisis question partly open: why pressure has become acute now and how financing/market and political constraints turn chronic deficits into crisis.

verbatim_comment: Useful fiscal explanation with a concrete spending decomposition. The shown evidence supports persistent deficits and high debt better than it establishes a present crisis. Clarify the stock-versus-ratio sequence and soften the exclusion of revenue explanations; repair the overlapping axis/source footers in charts 3 and 4. Sources, central arithmetic, underlying chart geometry and reproduction were not verified in this reading.
most_useful_improvement: Rewrite the main explanation around the debt stock versus debt/GDP ratio: replace “Between shocks it did not fall back” with the actual post-2020 decline, then distinguish the chronic fiscal problem from the separately evidenced financing or political pressures needed to answer why it is a crisis now. Keep the high-revenue comparison as an accounting contrast rather than a causal exclusion.
